For example, did you know Trump paid nearly $100k to take out a newspaper ad in 1987 arguing for tariffs on Japan and Saudi Arabia?

2.

My fifth post was—I thought—surely going to be the most controversial. It was inspired by ’s first book and ’s 2021 piece in American Affairs. To my surprise, though, I didn’t get any hate mail.

The worst I got was a former dean from another state chiding me for not citing Henry Louis Gates, Jr.—supposedly “the most important voice on the relationship of race history in America,” though when I asked what specific elements of his oeuvre I should have cited, the only reply I got was “All of it?”

This was a nice learning experience for me. First, I learned that my audience responds to high-effort, even-handed treatments of important topics. Second, I learned that a few critics just like to hear themselves complain.

3.

This one was a passion project, and it was my first time showing up on Daily Nous (one of the two big philosophy blogs). When I travel to new departments, there are always some grad students who say they enjoyed this piece, which means a lot to me.

Students are (literally) the future of any academic discipline, and the philosophy torch will be rather soggy unless the next generation feels inspired.

4.

Sometimes, there comes a time when one feels a moral-ethical-cloutological duty to post. This was one such time.

5.

I think this one aged pretty well.

If you always block people who disagree with you about important topics, you won’t end up following anyone intellectually independent of you. That’s bad: it means your sources will be like parrots in an echo chamber, rather than experts who can corroborate each other.

6.

Secretly an homage to . (Don’t tell him.)

7 & 8.

A duo written in the aftermath of Charlie Kirk’s assassination.

9.

My most popular piece by far. Some people read this as an all-out attack on Continental philosophy—it wasn’t! It was almost entirely a critique of two arguments given in defense of unclear writing.

As said in the comments, I didn’t pull punches. But I also tried to avoid overgeneralizations.

10.

Is this a work of enduring philosophical insight? — no.

Is this an intervention into a debate of public significance? — also no.

But did it make longtime reader audibly chuckle? — presumably yes.

We must imagine Sisyphus happy Amos chuckling.

Subscribe now

What will 2026 bring for Big iff True?

I’ve got some posts lined up on moral/political philosophy, of course, as well as game theory, social choice theory, graph theory, and even a little measurement theory. That’s a lot of theories! You can also expect a few roundups of empirical studies in economics, criminology, and/or political science, as well as the occasional piece on writing, speaking, or teaching.

But above all, I hope to keep Big iff True going as a venue for interdisciplinary conversations in the spirit of PPE—aka Philosophy, Politics, and Economics. As you may know, I’m a “Core Faculty” member in UNC’s PPE Program. And I want to close out my first year of blogging with my favorite tribute to interdisciplinary work.

This is an excerpt from a piece called “PPE as an Intellectual Enterprise,” by Geoff Sayre-McCord, a Distinguished Professor at UNC, and Geoff Brennan, a brilliant economist who taught at both UNC and the Australian National University.

Geoff Brennan and I spoke only twice: once in his office, where he welcomed me for a friendly chat before I left Australia for my job at UNC, and once on the phone while he was in hospice, where he told me he was spending his last weeks on earth on a PPE book called Back to Basics, which had been promised to the press an astonishing 15 years prior. Never too late for the basics, I say.2

Geoff Sayre-McCord, meanwhile, is the Director of UNC’s PPE Program and Founding Director of the PPE Society. For what it’s worth, I hold Geoff’s philosophical judgment in the absolute highest esteem. There just ain’t many like him.

So, without further ado (and with thanks to Geoff Sayre-McCord for his permission), let me share with you a passage from the Geoffs’ PPE paper, which we at UNC lovingly refer to as the Three Spotlights.

Anything that throws light on its subject matter also casts shadows. So much is just in the nature of light. And those shadows cannot be dispersed simply by increasing the intensity of the light: doing that just makes the shadows deeper. Of course, if the intensity of the light is reduced, so is the capacity to see anything clearly. If you want to illuminate the shadows, you have to come at things from different perspectives: you have to shine some light, simultaneously, from different angles. And as every theatre-lighting engineer knows, in order to establish a shadow-free stage, you have to secure an appropriate balance among the various light sources.

This picture animates our view of PPE – that is, Philosophy, Politics, and Economics – as an intellectual enterprise. Bringing philosophy, political science, and economics together in the study of social and political institutions sheds light and banishes shadows in ways that no subset of these three disciplines could possibly accomplish. For example, economists shed invaluable light on markets, efficiency, incentives, and trade-offs, but regularly ignore the formal and informal institutions that structure choices and social interdependence; and economists (almost as a matter of professional pride) steer clear of questions of rights, or justice, or value. Meanwhile, political scientists bring a deep understanding of institutions that structure choices and create social interdependence, along with their origin and structure and effect. Political scientists also explicitly consider positive rights and values as they find expression through and in those institutions. Yet, political scientists often leave to one side perverse incentives and markets (except as phenomena to be regulated or left alone) and questions concerning institutionally transcendent rights, justice, and values. Philosophers, of course, talk ad nauseam about rights, justice, and value, and they are fully engaged with questions concerning ideal political institutions and perfect markets, but they regularly ignore actual social and political institutions and how they work, or fail to work, and the incentives, perverse and otherwise, that they create.

It is worth emphasizing at the outset that this view of PPE is both pro- and counter-disciplinary.

It is pro-disciplinary in that it insists that disciplines are crucial sources of illumination and are indispensable. However, because the picture highlights what each of the disciplines (inevitably) occludes, it foregrounds the importance of reaching across disciplinary boundaries.

Here’s to another year of reaching.

Subscribe now

1

A criminally incomplete list of commenters: , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , and my RL friends Joe, Blaine, Travis, Kerah, Rahul, and Zac. Also my dad, , who gave me some great feedback on my Substack livestreams.

I have to finish off this post ASAP to leave for a vacation with my wife, otherwise the list would be longer!

2

Let me also shout out “Moving Towards the Median,” a 2024 paper about compulsory voting that Geoff Brennan wrote with my (outrageously smart) former colleague Alexandra Oprea, who finished the project after Geoff’s death. I love this paper—and what a beautiful tribute to Geoff from Alex.

item.title: Self-radicalizing theories
item.description: Joe Heath's critique of critical theory goes higher than you think.
item.content:encoded:
A conspiracy theorist dies and goes to heaven. After entering the Pearly Gates, he comes face to face with God, who embraces him and says,

“Welcome! As a reward for your good deeds on earth, I offer you this gift: the true answer to any question of your choice.”

The conspiracy theorist thinks for a moment and asks, “Who shot JFK?”

“Ah, a fine question,” God replies. “It was Lee Harvey Oswald, acting alone.”

“Incredible,” says the theorist. “This goes higher than I thought…”

You may have heard of cognitively closed systems—various isms that trap their adherents in an erroneous web of belief, systematically obscuring the path back to truth. Think of Plato’s Cave, Wittgenstein’s fly-bottle, or Hobbes’s bird stuck indoors, “fluttering at false light” (i.e. banging itself against the window rather than flying back out the chimney).

The philosopher/logician/mystic Raymond Smullyan gives a number of more modern (merely potential) examples, which I repeat here without endorsement: the Freudian who views every objection to psychoanalysis as the product of repressed desire; the Marxist who spurns all counterevidence as bourgeois ideology; the feminist who dismisses all critics as agents of the patriarchy; the solipsist who insists that his detractors are figments of his own imagination; and so on. To this, we could add the centrist whose critics are all “tribalists,” the capitalist whose critics are just “envious,” and the male incel whose critics are all “NPCs.”

In each case, you can see how the closed system (supposing it really is closed) works to insulate itself against legitimate critiques.

In “Problems in the Theory of Ideology”—a prescient paper from 2001— introduces a fascinating spin on the closed system: the self-radicalizing theory. The basic idea is that some theories tend to degenerate into more extreme versions of themselves over time, because they nudge their proponents to respond to valid counterevidence not by abandoning their theories, but by doubling, tripling, and eventually n-tupling down. The self-radicalizer ends up like the conspiracy theorist who, after being refuted by almighty God, concludes that even He must be in on it.

Subscribe now

Heath’s main example of the self-radicalizer is the “ideology critic,” a kind of social theorist who thinks of oppression as the result of a widespread cognitive error, typically blamed on the oppressors. The ideology critic looks around at the social world and sees that certain individuals—the working class, women, etc.—are collectively failing to promote their own interests; rather than locking arms in resistance, they’re mostly submitting to or even reinforcing an oppressive social system. What’s going on? “Why aren’t these people acting rationally?” wonders the critic. “The workers of the world should be uniting to overthrow the bourgeoisie, just as women should be coming together to overthrow the patriarchy!” The fact that this isn’t already happening cries out for explanation. And so the ideology critic explains the persistence of oppression as the result of a systematic belief in a pernicious “ideology”—some theory that deludes or tricks the oppressed class into reproducing the conditions of their own oppression. Think: “a woman’s status should be determined by her appearance,” or “rich people earn their riches through hard work and thriftiness.”

The problem with ideology critique, says Heath, is that it assumes cooperation is easy. The critic supposes that rational people generally would work together to promote their shared interests; so, when the proletariat (or whoever) fails to do so, we infer that they must be suffering from some kind of cognitive illusion—hence, ideology.

But cooperation isn’t easy! It’s perfectly normal for people to fail to promote their shared interests, even if everyone involved is acting rationally. This is called a “collective action problem,” and it can arise for a variety of well-known reasons, such as:

  • Misaligned incentives — often the socially beneficial action, like fighting for reform or refraining from pollution, is prohibitively costly for the individual who does it (the benefits, rather than being “internalized,” flow to “free riders”).

  • Lack of trust — some actions, like joining a revolution or switching industry standards, can be disastrous unless most people do it together; if no one has reason to trust that others will join, no one will risk going it alone.

  • Adapted preferences — poor/oppressed people may have preferences that are “adapted” to their low expectations, which can cause frustration when trying to “break out” of social roles, and which can be a disadvantage when bargaining with the rich/powerful.

It bears emphasizing that none of these explanations imply that the individuals involved are dumb or delusional. If anything, they’re victims of their own rationality! Cooperation would be easier if we all superstitiously assumed that we’d each be rewarded for pro-social actions, as if by moral magic.1

No wonder, then, that “ideology critique” has often led to disappointment. The workers still haven’t flocked to the ramparts even after decades of critical theory conferences; the gender pay gap still persists even after concepts like “patriarchy” have become so popular as to be the stuff of Hollywood cliché. The main prediction of ideology critique appears to have been refuted by experience. We have arrived at the moment when God pins the blame on Oswald.

But like the stubborn conspiracy theorist, the ideology critics would rather stick to their explanatory guns. Instead of looking for some other explanation beyond pure ideology, the critic instead concludes that they must have underestimated ideology, which turns out to be more pervasive and well-hidden than anyone expected. This goes higher than I thought.

Subscribe now

Thus begins the “vicious cycle of theoretical self-radicalization.” Here’s how Heath describes the process:

The more serious problem for critical theory arises as follows: after having presented the criticism, and having it widely accepted, the critic expects to see some kind of social change. When none is forthcoming, the critic begins to suspect, not that there is a practical problem preventing implementation of the desired improvements, but that the criticism itself was too superficial, that it didn’t get to the root of the problem. The ideology must be more pervasive than originally suspected. Perhaps the original criticism was insufficiently radical, because it used concepts that were in general circulation, and hence complicit in the ideological system. The solution may be to deconstruct these concepts, and form an entirely new set.

Once this line of thinking has been engaged, the critical theory becomes increasingly baroque, increasingly obscure, and of course, increasingly unlikely to change anything. This can generate a vicious cycle of theoretical self-radicalization, in which critics respond to the increasing irrelevance of their theories by further radicalizing them, making the entire apparatus more and more remote from the concerns and the vocabulary of everyday life. (p. 188)

If I may add own objection: as self-radicalizing theories grow more elaborate, they also tend to become more ambiguous, with the result that critics will increasingly be unable to agree about the content of the ideology they’re critiquing. Does patriarchy demand that women dress modestly (thus controlling their personal choices), or does it encourage women to wear revealing clothes (thus catering to the male gaze)? If there’s no clear answer, then citing patriarchal ideology isn’t going to do much to explain real-world outcomes.

So, whether you’re worried about women’s rights or workers’ wellbeing, Heath thinks you should at least eventually try to analyze the problem as a normal failure of collective action rather than an overcomplicated triumph of ideology. Think of Claudia Goldin’s Nobel-winning work on the gender pay gap, or Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson’s Nobel-winning critique of “extractive institutions.” It’s the 21st century: we’re living in a golden age of empirical methods and sitting on a gold mine of wisdom about collective action problems (courtesy of 20th-century social science). There’s really no need to theoretically radicalize yourself into irrelevance.

But enough prelude! I’m not here to defend Heath’s (admittedly interesting) view of ideology. I’m more interested in his concept of self-radicalization, which is fascinating in its own right, and which applies across a wide range of intellectual contexts. The key is to notice that Heath’s giving an informal example of what scientists call a dynamical explanation. If you wanted to make it a bit more formal, you might put it like this.

We assume that people choose from a variety of different belief systems, but they change their beliefs only gradually, as they try to remove tensions and contradictions; people don’t just spontaneously convert to a completely different worldview. The space of all possible belief systems is called a “configuration space,” and the amount of tension in a system is its level of “energy.” The key methodological assumption is that people will change their beliefs iff there’s a sufficiently close belief system with lower energy. Simplifying (because I suck at thinking in 4+ dimensions), we can draw the configuration space as a 2D grid, which allows us to plot the energy levels as a curvy shape floating overhead, like so:

Now we have a beautiful, simple model of how a person’s beliefs develop over time. Like a marble rolling to the bottom of a bowl, a person’s belief system continuously develops towards the local minimum of tension and dissonance. The problem, as you can see in the above diagram, is that the local minimum isn’t always the global minimum. A believer might end up trapped—there’s a better location on the other side of the configuration space, but there’s no way to get there without “rolling uphill.”

This is how I think of the self-radicalizer: they’re stuck in a bad local minimum. Each time they resolve a tension in their worldview by making themselves more extreme, they are tragically moving away from the best possible viewpoint and towards a far more mediocre equilibrium that just happens to be closer to where they started. The only way out is to somehow shake things up—think of Brian Eno’s Oblique Strategies, cards designed to jolt you out of a cognitive rut.

Where else do we see self-radicalization? Some examples:

  • Echo chambers — on some difficult topics, we have to rely on experts to figure out what’s going on. But as Thi Nguyen warns, “our inexpertise may lead us to pick out bad experts, which will simply reinforce our mistaken beliefs and sensibilities.” We thus end up in a “runaway echo chamber,” where we distrust the very sources most able to correct us.

  • Cults — yeah, I’m linking to Thi Nguyen twice in a row, but it’s not my fault he’s interesting. As Nguyen puts it, an echo chamber can be like a cult, which “isolates its members by actively alienating them from any outside sources. Those outside are actively labelled as malign and untrustworthy. A cult member’s trust is narrowed, aimed with laser-like focus on certain insider voices.” Distrust of outsiders then creates “a social buffer against any attempts to extract the indoctrinated person from the cult.” Those who dip their toes into the cult quickly end up completely submerged.

  • Conspiracy theories — not to repeat myself, but often a conspiracy theory will include some suspiciously convenient tenet designed to discredit nonbelievers. (Say it with me: This goes higher than I thought.) See also: “The Devil put the fossils in the ground to deceive you,” which is a thing I was taught at my religious afterschool program in 4th grade. (Really.)

  • Bigotry — a bigot believes that their in-group is superior to some out-group, which naturally inclines the bigot towards in-group socializing and out-group distrust. This tends to insulate them from disconfirming evidence and sweep them up in group-polarized deliberations. (The group may even evolve metanorms, so that members are punished if they don’t enforce in-group solidarity—Axelrod gives the example of white people who were violently attacked by other whites for refusing to participate in a lynch mob.) Thus someone who starts out with mild in-group preferences can end up self-radicalizing into a hardcore racist, sexist, anti-semite, etc., utterly detached from reality.

Something that all of these worldviews have in common is that they’re Manichean. Once you buy into them, you begin to distrust those who lack the view (since they’re bad, evil outsiders). Then you buy into the Manichean worldview even more, which means you distrust the outsiders even more, and so on.

The possibility of self-radicalization seems to me a structural danger in any Manichean view. I hesitate to call it a defect, however, since it’s possible that some Manichean view might actually be true, in which case it’s good if that particular view is self-radicalizing.

Consider our own (good) beliefs about the law of induction, according to which the future will tend to be like the past. We assume that the laws of physics that worked up until today will continue working tomorrow; we don’t expect things to randomly change in never-before-seen patterns. Given that we believe in induction, the continued success of inductive reasoning seems like ever more evidence in its favor; our inductive worldview is self-radicalizing. But imagine we’d instead started out believing in counter-induction, according to which the future tends to be unlike the past. Then we would’ve ended up in a quite different equilibrium, as in the old fable.

A philosopher travels to a distant village where everyone reasons by counter-induction. Every night, their gurus predict that the sun will not rise tomorrow, and every morning, they suffer a humiliating refutation.

One day the philosopher can’t help but ask the elder guru, “Why do you keep using counter-induction? Haven’t you noticed it’s failed you every day?”

“Of course!” replies the guru. “That’s why it’s bound to work tomorrow.”

Subscribe now

One last potential upside. In general, self-radicalizing does seem pretty bad. But in certain contexts, even if it’s individually costly, I wonder if it might be socially beneficial.

This seems to be what Ian Shaprio thinks of Jeremy Bentham’s version of utilitarianism, the view that we should always do whatever maximizes global happiness. Bentham’s view is infamously extreme—no special treatment for loved ones; no natural rights; etc.—but it’s also beautifully pure. Because Bentham pursues his core idea to its logical conclusions, rather than adulterating it in hopes of arriving at more respectable conclusions, Bentham teaches us something deep about what that core idea really contains, even if the contents aren’t ultimately correct.

Here’s Shapiro:

There are some thinkers in the Western tradition—I guess in any tradition—who have a particular characteristic that Bentham certainly has, and I think…Karl Marx had and Robert Nozick had. And the thing I’m thinking of here is they are the kind of person who takes one idea to the most extreme possible formulation. They ask themselves a question, “How would the world be if this idea that I have is the only important idea?” and they take it to its logical extreme, to an excessive kind of formulation.

And they will go places with their idea that nobody else will go, and so that makes them a little bit crazy. They’re monomaniacal, obsessively consumed with their idea. …

But what’s always interesting about people like this is that they play out an idea to its logical extreme, and that exhibits both its strengths and its limitations, just because they’re willing to go when others will not go—think the unthinkable, think politically incorrect things for their time—in pursuit of really pushing this idea to the absolute hilt.

And so Bentham is the kind of thinker who I suspect, at the end of the day, nobody will be fully convinced by, but he’s very useful. He’s a very useful diagnostician of what it is about utilitarianism that’s going to be appealing to you, and where eventually you’re going to want to put some limits on it, just because he goes beyond the limits.

The point isn’t that Bentham’s pure view is more plausible than a more moderate version of utilitarianism—such as a “consequentialized” hybrid. While I do like that point, Shapiro’s saying something else: even granting that Bentham’s extreme view is less plausible, it might be more revealing. Bentham pays the price of implausibility so that we can enjoy the benefit of understanding what True Utilitarianism looks like. In terms of our dynamical model, a monomaniac like Bentham can be seen as an intrepid explorer of the configuration space.

I may not always follow in your footsteps, intrepid explorers. But I do salute you.

Subscribe now

1

There are also plenty of respectable worldviews that grease the wheels of cooperation through a kind of cosmic, pro-social ideology. According to some religions, for example, the afterlife will sort out the misalignment of mundane incentives: you are rewarded (or punished) after death in proportion to the good (or evil) you did beforehand.

Compare this to the much sillier Aristotelian view that, whenever we act virtuously, that is in our best earthly interests. (The soldier who dies for his country, says Aristotle, is better off dying in a blaze of glory than retreating in shame.) You can see hints of this view in the “prosperity gospel,” according to which God rewards believers with blessings during their worldly lives. This is a particularly interesting doctrine because it makes empirical predictions that should be amenable to econometric confirmation. Get on it, economists!

(Related fact: Robert Barro and Rachel McCleary have a classic paper about religious belief and economic growth. Their findings suggest that belief in heaven and hell causes more economic growth, but attending church has the opposite effect!)

item.title: Jay Powell and the rule of law
item.description: It’s the goose that lays the golden egg. Are we about to flush it down the golden toilet?
item.content:encoded:
Jerome Powell has been working for the Federal Reserve since before I could legally drink. In 2012, President Obama nominated him to the Fed’s Board of Governors. Six years later, President Trump elevated him to Chair of the Federal Reserve, the high perch to which he was reappointed by President Biden in 2021.

Now, Powell is under criminal investigation for reasons that are, frankly, difficult to take at face value. Federal prosecutors are investigating Powell over his testimony to Congress regarding the renovation of the Federal Reserve’s office buildings, a project that President Trump has derided as “excessive.”

Does anyone seriously think that Donald J. Trump—who has decorated the Oval Office with gilded trim, appliqués, and antiques; who has remodeled the Lincoln Bathroom with marble and gold; whose name is synonymous with glitzy real estate— is morally committed to thrifty renovations? The question answers itself. (Indeed, some years ago, Trump’s own appointees to a project review board had recommended that the Fed use more marble.)

Subscribe now

Critics fear that Trump is aiming to undermine the independence of the Fed in order to gain more control over monetary policy. In a nutshell: the Fed has powers that, if exercised well, are supposed to keep inflation low and employment high. But those powers can also be used to heat up the economy, producing short-term gains and long-term pain (in the form of excruciatingly high inflation). Because it is so tempting for politicians to abuse those powers in the lead-up to elections, the Fed has the power to operate independently.

To many economists, including Powell himself, the new criminal investigation is a serious threat to Fed independence and—even more importantly—to the rule of law.1 In this post, I want to share some notable reactions to this news, starting with Powell’s own statement on January 11.

Good evening.

On Friday, the Department of Justice served the Federal Reserve with grand jury subpoenas, threatening a criminal indictment related to my testimony before the Senate Banking Committee last June. That testimony concerned in part a multi-year project to renovate historic Federal Reserve office buildings.

I have deep respect for the rule of law and for accountability in our democracy. No one—certainly not the chair of the Federal Reserve—is above the law. But this unprecedented action should be seen in the broader context of the administration’s threats and ongoing pressure.

This new threat is not about my testimony last June or about the renovation of the Federal Reserve buildings. It is not about Congress’s oversight role; the Fed through testimony and other public disclosures made every effort to keep Congress informed about the renovation project. Those are pretexts. The threat of criminal charges is a consequence of the Federal Reserve setting interest rates based on our best assessment of what will serve the public, rather than following the preferences of the President.

This is about whether the Fed will be able to continue to set interest rates based on evidence and economic conditions—or whether instead monetary policy will be directed by political pressure or intimidation.

I have served at the Federal Reserve under four administrations, Republicans and Democrats alike. In every case, I have carried out my duties without political fear or favor, focused solely on our mandate of price stability and maximum employment. Public service sometimes requires standing firm in the face of threats. I will continue to do the job the Senate confirmed me to do, with integrity and a commitment to serving the American people.

Thank you.

shared the video at Marginal Revolution with the title:

The price of gold went vertical

followed up at MR with a less Straussian post:

Whether an independent Fed is desirable is beside the point. The core issue is lawfare: the strategic use of legal processes to intimidate, constrain, and punish institutional actors for political ends. Lawfare is the hallmark of a failing state because it erodes not just political independence, but the capacity for independent judgment.

What sort of people will work at the whim of another? The inevitable result is toadies and ideological loyalists heading complex institutions, rather than people chosen for their knowledge and experience.

Other economic commentators, including some who are not sympathetic to Powell’s views, are also saying they agree about “Trump’s motivation.”

In a coup for Substack (I see you, ), a truly stacked bipartisan group of economic heavy-hitters posted a “Statement Regarding the Federal Reserve” here on this platform. It reads:

The Federal Reserve’s independence and the public’s perception of that independence are critical for economic performance, including achieving the goals Congress has set for the Federal Reserve of stable prices, maximum employment, and moderate long-term interest rates. The reported criminal inquiry into Federal Reserve Chair Jay Powell is an unprecedented attempt to use prosecutorial attacks to undermine that independence. This is how monetary policy is made in emerging markets with weak institutions, with highly negative consequences for inflation and the functioning of their economies more broadly. It has no place in the United States whose greatest strength is the rule of law, which is at the foundation of our economic success.

As of 1/13 (the day after it was first posted, signatories include Ben Bernanke, Janet Yellen, and Allan Greenspan—among other major figures in the Fed’s history.

In my state of North Carolina, we are represented by the Republican Senator Thom Tillis, an important figure for several reasons. Senator Tillis sits on the Senate Banking Committe, where the Republicans have only a slim 13-11 majority; even one defection would give the Democrats enough votes to tie. Senator Tillis was also one of only two Republican Senators to vote against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act—and after breaking with Pres. Trump’s signature bill, Tillis announced he would not seek reelection in 2026.

On January 11, Senator Tillis’s office released this statement regarding the news about Jay Powell:

If there were any remaining doubt whether advisers within the Trump Administration are actively pushing to end the independence of the Federal Reserve, there should now be none. It is now the independence and credibility of the Department of Justice that are in question.

I will oppose the confirmation of any nominee for the Fed—including the upcoming Fed Chair vacancy—until this legal matter is fully resolved.

What to make of all this?

I suppose it is conceivable that Jay Powell said something untrue to Congress about the $2.5 billion renovation of the Fed’s offices. That price tag does seem high, prima facie. But the Fed’s offices are historical buildings with significant amounts of asbestos and lead. Renovating old buildings is notoriously expensive in the US: it’s not cheap to comply with newer codes and laws, such as the Americans with Disabilities Act, nor is it easy to predict how much toxic stuff is waiting to be discovered in the pipes and insulation. In a country where a new public bathroom can be priced at $1.7 million, a high price tag isn’t proof of foul play.

Another relevant piece of evidence is that President Trump has, in the past, made reckless accusations about the Fed’s renovations. Here he is last July—in a truly remarkable exchange—claiming that the expected cost of renovations just “went up a little bit” from $2.7 to $3.1 billion. “I’m not aware of that,” Powell sharply replies. “It just came out,” says Trump, retrieving a piece of paper from his suit pocket. Powell puts on his reading glasses, peruses the paper, and notes that the $3.1B figure is only higher because it includes the cost of renovations for the Martin Building—which had been completed years ago. Trump then calls the Martin building “a building that’s being built.”

Here Trump’s accusations are “unconnected to a concern with truth,” to borrow a phrase from Harry Frankfurt. This only lends weight to Powell’s contention that the accusations against him are a pretext, meant to clear the way for a more compliant Fed Chair willing to satisfy Trump’s desire for rate cuts.

Powell is right on the principle: no one should be above the law—not even the president.

“In a perfect theocracy,” writes David Hume, people would be governed “by particular volitions” of an omniscient being, rather than general laws that bind everyone. James Madison echoes Hume in Federalist 51: “If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary.”

Alas, Americans aren’t governed by perfect angels, but by humans: a cohort of fallible, finite beings who make it first past the post on election day. For that reason we need some constraints on government. We do not want to be ruled by people who enjoy arbitrary “powers to coerce particular people for the purposes they choose,” as Friedrich Hayek puts it in The Constitution of Liberty.

Those who would defend the investigation of Powell owe it to the rest of the country to give us a plausible argument—or else come clean and admit to having abandoned concern for the rule of law.

Subscribe now

1

The investigation of Powell echoes an earlier attempt to fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook. The President can only fire a Fed Governor “for cause,” not on a whim. President Trump therefore alleged that Cook had committed mortgage fraud, but he wasn’t able to produce sufficient evidence to back up this allegation in federal court, where Judge Jia Cobb issued a preliminary injunction against Cook’s firing, writing that “Cook has made a strong showing that her purported removal was done in violation of the Federal Reserve Act’s ‘for cause’ provision.”

item.title: The last founding father
item.content:encoded:
Subscribe now

You probably know the basics about MLK, Jr.

King was born on Janurary 15, 1929 to a Baptist family in Atlanta, GA. From ages 3–6, King was close friends with a white boy—whose father eventually forbade the friendship.1 King attended Morehouse College from 1944–1948, then Crozier Seminary until 1951, and finally to Boston University for his Doctorate, which he received in 1955. King moved to Montgomery to preach, where he became the leader of the celebrated Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–1956) kicked off by Rosa Parks, Jo Ann Robinson, and other local activists. During that time, King got to know a small group of advisors from New York: Ella Baker, Bayard Rustin, and Stanley Levison. After the boycott’s success, they founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference in early 1957, which became the central institution through which King achieved so many stunning victories for civil rights, such as the Civil Rights Act of 1964, made possible by the Birmingham Campaign and March on Washington in 1963, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, made possible by the dramatic Selma to Montgomery Marches earlier that year. After those bills became law, King began to shift his focus towards economic justice and foreign policy. Against the advice of Rustin and Levison, King spoke out against the Vietnam War, which he opposed in part because of his longstanding commitment to nonviolence, and in part because of his having won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964. Finally, on April 4, 1968, King was shot in the cheek and shoulder as he was leaving for dinner from the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, TN; the doctors pronounced him dead barely an hour later.

He was 39 years old.

MLK’s achievements were, of course, enormously inspiring. But his life was also shot through with anguish and tragedy. King was underslept, overworked, constantly under extraordinary pressure, constantly under attack. Within the Civil Rights Movement, he was the object of petty sniping; jealous rivals called him “De Lawd” behind his back and “mister big” to his face.2 Black nationalists like Malcolm X called him a “modern Uncle Tom.” Towards the end of his life, King was haunted by a sense that he would soon be killed. When the assassin’s bullet finally did come for King—the greatest advocate of nonviolence in American history—the country erupted into riots.3 Richard Nixon won that year’s election; the Vietnam War shambled on; and King’s coalition never won a great victory for economic justice on the scale of the Civil Rights Acts.

Today, we know King as an American hero—a founding father, as Jonathan Eig puts it. But no hero is guaranteed to be recognized as such, and any hero is in danger of being forgotten, or of having their legacy distorted and betrayed.

In light of all this, I think it’s wonderful that Americans celebrate Martin Luther King, Jr. Day—and I do mean celebrate. It’s great that we can remind ourselves of the basics of King’s contributions to the country, and I can’t think of a better way to honor his legacy than to look for glimmers of hope amidst some of the bleakest chapters of our history.

So for anyone interested in King’s life and career, here is a chance to test your knowledge (and perhaps learn a fun fact or two).

MLK Day Quiz

Q1. Why was King chosen to be the leader of the Montgomery Bus Boycott?

Q2. Did King ever meet Malcolm X?

Q3. What was King’s full name at birth?

Q4. Who approved the FBI’s wiretap of MLK? (When?)

Q5. What was the big protest King was planning at the time of his death?

Q6. King’s interest in the Vietnam War was stimulated by pictures in what magazine?

Q7. Where did King give his “I Have a Dream” speech? (Had it been given before?)

Q8. Who else in King’s family had preached at Ebeneezer Baptist Church in Atlanta?

Q9. Coretta Scott King advocated for MLK Day. When was it first celebrated?

Q10. What was the last speech MLK delivered? (Where?)

Answers

Q1. King was chosen in part because he was so new to town. That meant he wasn’t seen as being aligned with any particular faction of preachers against the others. Also notable is that—unlike Jo Ann Robinson, a professor at a public university—King’s income couldn’t be taken away by the government in retaliation.

Q2. King did meet Malcolm X, though only once: it was on March 26, 1964 in Washington, DC, during the filibuster of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

Q3. King was born Michael King, Jr.—his father changed both their names after a trip to Germany.

Q4. RFK approved the first official wiretap of MLK on October 10, 1963. But the FBI had already been able to listen in on King through their tap on Stanley Levison. (For a detailed discussion of Levison’s ties to—and turn away from—the Communist Party, see Beverly Gage’s G-Man.)

Q5. King was planning what he called the Poor People’s March (aka the Poor People’s Campaign), a version of which took place over the summer of 1968 with little success.

Q6. Ramparts—in particular, a January 1967 photo essay called “The Children of Vietnam.”

Q7. At the March on Washington on August 28, 1963. King had given the speech in Detroit in June of that year, and even as far back as November 1962 in North Carolina.

Q8. King was the third-generation at Ebeneezer: his father and maternal grandfather both preached there.

Q9. 1986, three years after Pres. Reagan signed the bill making it an official federal holiday.

Q10. “I’ve Been to the Mountaintop” in Memphis TN on April 3, 1968—just one day before his death.

All we say to America is, “Be true to what you said on paper.” If I lived in China or even Russia, or any totalitarian country, maybe I could understand some of these illegal injunctions. Maybe I could understand the denial of certain basic First Amendment privileges, because they hadn’t committed themselves to that over there. But somewhere I read—of the freedom of assembly. Somewhere I read—of the freedom of speech. Somewhere I read—of the freedom of press. Somewhere I read—that the greatness of America is the right to protest for rights.

And so just as I say, we aren’t going to let dogs or water hoses turn us around, we aren’t going to let any injunction turn us around. We are going on.

Well, I don’t know what will happen now. We’ve got some difficult days ahead. But it really doesn’t matter with me now, because I’ve been to the mountaintop.

And I don’t mind. Like anybody, I would like to live a long life. Longevity has its place. But I’m not concerned about that now. I just want to do God’s will. And He’s allowed me to go up to the mountain. And I’ve looked over. And I’ve seen the Promised Land. I may not get there with you. But I want you to know tonight, that we, as a people, will get to the promised land.

And so I’m happy, tonight. I’m not worried about anything. I’m not fearing any man. Mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord!

Subscribe now

Share

That’s it! Hope you enjoyed the quiz, and please let me know if you have any feedback or suggestions for future posts on MLK, one of the greatest American leaders of all time, and one of freedom’s greatest champions.

Got any fun MLK facts or favorite MLK speeches? Share them in the comments!

Leave a comment

1

From Chapter 1 of MLK’s autobiography:

From the age of three I had a white playmate who was about my age. We always felt free to play our childhood games together. He did not live in our community, but he was usually around every day; his father owned a store across the street from our home. At the age of six we both entered school—separate schools, of course. I remember how our friendship began to break as soon as we entered school; this was not my desire but his. The climax came when he told me one day that his father had demanded that he would play with me no more. I never will forget what a great shock this was to me. I immediately asked my parents about the motive behind such a statement.

We were at the dinner table when the situation was discussed, and here for the first time I was made aware of the existence of a race problem. I had never been conscious of it before. As my parents discussed some of the tragedies that had resulted from this problem and some of the insults they themselves had confronted on account of it, I was greatly shocked, and from that moment on I was determined to hate every white person. As I grew older and older this feeling continued to grow.

My parents would always tell me that I should not hate the white man, but that it was my duty as a Christian to love him. The question arose in my mind: How could I love a race of people who hated me and who had been responsible for breaking me up with one of my best childhood friends? This was a great question in my mind for a number of years.

2

The “mister big” quote is from a memorable outburst by Fred Shuttlesworth, who was outraged by the news that King had struck a one-day truce:

“Tell President Kennedy he doesn’t live down here, and I live down here, and the people trust us, and we’re not calling the demonstrations off, no matter who calls you. Tell him King can’t call it off, tell him he can’t call it off, tell him I ain’t going to call it off … I’m going home.” King struggled to salvage the situation. “Wait a minute, Fred.” Turning to [Assistant AG] Marshall, King said, “We got to have unity, Burke. We’ve just got to have unity.” Shuttlesworth’s feelings were not assuaged. “I’ll be damned if you’ll have it like this. You’re mister big, but you’re going to be mister S-H-I-T. I’m sorry, but I cannot compromise my principles and the principles that we established.” With that, Shuttlesworth walked out.

From David J. Garrow, Bearing the Cross, Ch. 5.

3

King had a nuanced view of riots. Just three weeks before his death, King gave a speech called “The Other America” at Grosse Pointe High School, in which he called a riot “the language of the unheard.”

Now I wanted to say something about the fact that we have lived over these last two or three summers with agony and we have seen our cities going up in flames. And I would be the first to say that I am still committed to militant, powerful, massive, non­-violence as the most potent weapon in grappling with the problem from a direct action point of view. I'm absolutely convinced that a riot merely intensifies the fears of the white community while relieving the guilt. And I feel that we must always work with an effective, powerful weapon and method that brings about tangible results.

But it is not enough for me to stand before you tonight and condemn riots. It would be morally irresponsible for me to do that without, at the same time, condemning the contingent, intolerable conditions that exist in our society. These conditions are the things that cause individuals to feel that they have no other alternative than to engage in violent rebellions to get attention. And I must say tonight that a riot is the language of the unheard. And what is it America has failed to hear? It has failed to hear that the plight of the negro poor has worsened over the last twelve or fifteen years. It has failed to hear that the promises of freedom and justice have not been met. And it has failed to hear that large segments of white society are more concerned about tranquility and the status quo than about justice and humanity.

That wasn’t the first time King had given this speech. He had given it about a year earlier at Stanford, saying that “In the final analysis, a riot is the language of the unheard.”

item.title: Don’t trash the humanities
item.description: In an era of AI and budget cuts, the humanities are getting dumped. To survive, we need to recommit to the inherent value of reading and writing.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the first ever guest post at Big iff True!

I’m delighted to share this piece by Kerah Gordon-Solmon, Associate Professor of Philosophy at Queen’s University — and one of my favorite philosophers in the game.

If you’d like to see more guests, let me know in the comments.

Leave a comment

It is a truth universally acknowledged that this is terrible moment for higher education — especially the humanities. AI mission creep is one culprit. Budgetary strain is another. They function in tandem like the trash compactor in the original Star Wars — grinding to an inevitable crunch.

We could weather one without the other. AI first: the extent to which students can too easily outsource their writing and reading to generative AI is extensively documented. But (and I write with certain pride in my colleagues), many of us are problem solving around it, not eliminating but containing its harms.

Examples: in my own teaching, I’ve weighted attendance more heavily than any other component. I keep track by having students hand-write and submit a reflection on our discussion every meeting. Screens are prohibited. For a decent course grade students must, at minimum, show up and pay enough attention to have something to write down. I’ve experimented with oral assessments: a group oral midterm (worthwhile) and individual essay oral defences (gloriously worthwhile). A chorus of us are demanding page citations in essays. These matter for reasons beyond hall monitoring. AI-generated text is a buffer between human users and original sources. Exact citations are a connective thread to those sources; they enable others to retrace one’s steps through them. They connote authority.

The intention is not only to offset the incentives nudging students toward AI-cheating, but also to anticipate what will mark someone as educated in an AI-drenched world. It’s a reasonable bet that this will be oracy skills — speaking and listening, live in real time.

So, I don’t believe generative AI is, by itself, an existential threat to humanities education, at least not yet. The problem is the best solutions are predicated on in-person interaction, and that only scales with commensurate resources. We have options in a class of 25 or 60 that we lose with higher numbers. Individual essay oral defences: doable for 30 students. Group oral midterms: doable for 60 students. And so forth.

This is where budget cuts devastate. At Queen’s University (where I teach in the Philosophy department) cutting costs means cutting faculty, and concomitantly, increasing student-to-faculty ratios. Tactics include hiring freezes, incentivizing early retirement for senior faculty, and reducing adjunct teaching positions — while clawing back TA funding and striking lower-enrolment courses from the books.

The upshot: our best strategies for mitigating the threat from AI are being systemically undermined by the institutional response to budget pressures.

Subscribe now

Our administration (like so many others) enjoins us to stop worrying and embrace AI in our teaching: do less with less; be ‘the university for the future [sic]’; advance the ‘strategic goal’ of ‘leveraging new technologies...so as better to prepare students to have impact in their chosen careers.’

These urgings are rooted in a conception of the university as a market actor. Our job is, first, to deliver a product our student-clients want, and second, to yield products (that is, graduates) employers will want to hire. It is, third, to serve society, e.g. through medical research. The focus is on the instrumental value of the university, its usefulness as a means to achieving valuable ends.

But being useful is not the only way of being valuable. There is intrinsic value, which is what we have in mind when we speak of the value of human life. There is also constitutive value, which refers to being an integral part of a valuable whole.

Elaborating on these is worth the digression. The significance of intrinsic value, in contrast with instrumental, comes out in thinking about our relationships with other people. We want our friends to value us for ourselves, and not because (say) they know we’ll always pay their way or get them into good parties. If we found out a friend only valued us for those reasons, we would feel used (or, instrumentalized). The “friendship” would be over.

Constitutive value presents more subtly. We invoke it when we praise something as ‘more than the sum of its parts.’ Think of an iconic music track with multiple instruments in its arrangement (any genre will do). If you isolate a single instrument’s contribution, it might not sound special or memorable. But the track would be the worse without it. This is constitutive value: it’s not freestanding, and it’s perceptible only in the context of the whole. It’s the introvert among the ways of being valuable.

What happens when we view universities as sites of intrinsic and constitutive, alongside instrumental, value?

The historical university goes back centuries, endowing us with centuries’ worth of accumulated scholarship and disciplinary practices. Contemporary universities are the collective bearer of that legacy. This confers a responsibility to preserve it, not only through research, but also through conferring onto new generations of students the knowledge and skills to appreciate and carry it forward, themselves.

The philosopher Agnes Callard writes of this eloquently:

In my early twenties, I entered a doctoral program in Classics at Berkeley.... I fought through thousands of pages of translation; I composed Greek prose in the style of Herodotus, Demosthenes, and Plato; I wrote about symbolism in Horatian Odes; I memorized dates and places for history exams; I learned Italian.... I became a citizen of a place that vanished thousands of years ago.... [A] feeling I remember vividly from that time is gratitude. Generation after generation of scribes had, as I saw it, copied those manuscripts for me, so that I could eventually read them. And this gratitude gave rise to a sense of responsibility: I too was a kind of scribe, tasked with keeping these texts available to and relevant for a new generation.

I enjoyed a frisson of recognition and appreciation reading this passage (and recommend the uncut original for its full effect). I want to pound the table and declare: “Intrinsic value!” But I’ll dig deeper, to the wellspring of the experience Callard describes.

No two academics will locate that wellspring in the same place. In surveying the ground for this piece, I kept rereading excerpts from two novels. (I could not have said why, except I felt compelled.) I reproduce those excerpts here, in abridged form.

The first is a descriptive passage from A.S. Byatt’s Still Life:

He considered the tree.

It had a dense, disorderly sheaf of twigs and suckers round the base of its trunk, and between these, and indeed under them, for many of them were attached above ground, the great, rigid, gripping lumps of the roots grasped the earth and went into it. He looked up the trunk which rose, scarred, cracked, knobby, and yet essentially direct into the air, a deliquescent trunk which forked and forked again into many repeated trunks, reaching or travelling up. This solid fountain had multiple crowns of thick secondary limbs, dividing into long twigs, fine twigs, leaflets, leaves, shoots.

He knew there was an inner geometry: Jacqueline had showed him drawings of the cambium layer: but he began to see an outer geometry.

Carefully contemplated, the growth of leaves from twigs, twigs from limbs, limbs from bole, showed to a geometric eye a persisting regularity in all this gnarled idiosyncrasy. The leaves grew out of the twigs in alternate ranks, at 180° from each other, and the twigs too could be mapped — given broken ends, scars, variations in girth, blemishes — as growing out of the branches on a regular spiral at the same angle. Marcus stared and mapped, stared and mapped, learning the tree.

The tree seen was solid geometry, meeting light. The tree, thought about, was contained and moving force and energy, stable yet changing.... Jacqueline had said apple trees drank four gallons per tree per hour. The water rose, not through suction, nor from pressure, but because it was an uninterrupted cohesive column, drawn up from base to crown. For a moment he saw the geometric fountain of rising water, a twisting and branching rope, the inner figure — no, an inner figure, there must be many — of its life and shape.

Light travelled from the sun at 186,000 miles per second, and the green he saw was refracted light, for the chlorophyll absorbed the red and blue-violet waves from the sun. The green was the light the tree did not consume. He saw in his mind’s eye the drama of the tree, the undifferentiated light pouring, silently, at terrible speed, meeting the solid rising column of water in the living and dead form of the tree.

Geometry he saw. The water, the properties of light, he knew. He must learn more. Plain curiosity is simpler and clearer than desire, and closer to life....

The second excerpt is a stretch of conversation among academics in a social setting, from Dorothy L. Sayers’s Gaudy Night. The conversation has turned to practical conflicts of values:

‘How about the artist of genius who has to choose between letting his family starve and painting pot-boilers to keep them?’

‘Well — he could stop painting. That, if he really is a genius, would be a loss to the world. But he mustn’t paint bad pictures — that would be really immoral.’

‘Why?’ asked Miss Edwards. ‘What do a few bad pictures matter, more or less?’

‘Of course they matter,’ said Miss Shaw. ‘A bad picture by a good painter is a betrayal of truth — his own truth.’

‘If you can’t agree about painters, make it someone else,’ [said Harriet]. ‘Make it a scientist.’

‘To take a concrete instance— ‘ [said Wimsey] ‘somebody wrote a novel called The Search —’

[‘I read it’] said the Dean. ‘It’s about a man who starts out to be a scientist and gets on very well till, just as he’s going to be appointed to an important executive post, he finds he’s made a careless error in a scientific paper. Somebody finds out, and he doesn’t get the job. So he decides he doesn’t really care about science after all.’

‘But,’ said Miss Chilperic, ‘if it was only a mistake—’

‘The point about it,’ said Wimsey, ‘is what an elderly scientist says to him. “The only ethical principle which has made science possible is that the truth shall be told all the time. If we do not penalise false statements made in error, we open up the way for false statements by intention. And a false statement of fact, made deliberately, is the most serious crime a scientist can commit.”

‘In the same novel,’ said the Dean, ‘somebody deliberately falsifies a result – later on, I mean – in order to get a job. And the man who made the original mistake finds it out. But he says nothing, because the other man is very badly off and has a wife and family to keep.’

‘[D]oes anybody here approve? A false statement is published and the man who could correct it lets it go, out of charitable considerations. Would anybody here do that?’

‘Of course one couldn’t do that,’ said Miss Barton. ‘Not for ten wives and fifty children.’

The first, Byatt, passage unfurls an epiphany, experienced mid-novel by a teenage boy. Marcus is intensely introverted, hyper-sensitive to sensory stimuli, and a former child math prodigy who retains an intuitive sense of geometry. He is alone in an elm grove, staring at one of the trees. As he looks, it morphs from being visually overwhelming, even threatening, into a coherent, intricate world unto itself. It reveals itself partway to his understanding, and invites — entices — both a state of detached contemplation and a commitment to its renewed, expanded study.

The shift in vision happens when he overlays his intuitive perception of the tree’s geometry onto facts he has learned (from his friend Jacqueline) about its biology. This is the holy grail of academic study: one’s internal capacities (and propensities) react with knowledge one has acquired to light up something outside of oneself — to reveal it as potentially endlessly interesting, and accessible to investigation, which it spurs. This is a vivified but detached way of seeing: one is lit up, oneself, with ‘plain curiosity’; one’s personal concerns and desires (and so forth) are sifted out.

The Sayers passage is completely different in content and tone. It features an after-dinner conversation amongst academics (plus one detective and one novelist) in a fictional Oxford women’s college in the 1930s. The conversation has turned to conflicts between worldly commitments (feeding one’s family), and fidelity to the truth in scientific research. The assembled are unanimously on the side of truth — not only in science, but as a grounding principle in all academic research, even painting. (Truth in painting is flagged as the ‘truth’ of one’s aesthetic vision: ‘he mustn’t paint bad pictures — that would be really immoral.’)

I plant my flag in these literary cloisters. The deepest source of universities’ intrinsic value is our commitment, first, to enabling the luminescent quality of vision Byatt conjures, and second, to cultivating, and holding ourselves accountable to, an ethos of pursuing the objects of that vision with exacting care and fidelity.

The institutional university has a responsibility to provide a conducive and protected habitat.

Subscribe now

This responsibility implies an imperative. One can hardly open a newspaper or magazine (print or digital) without encountering a think piece on the decline of literacy among university students. Reading complex texts, never mind old, long, complex texts, is portrayed increasingly as beyond their capacity. Similar points are being made about students’ writing abilities. AI is not the cause, but it is an accelerant.

A university’s purpose is to produce, disseminate, and preserve knowledge. We produce it through original research, disseminate it by publishing and teaching, and preserve it through archival work and, again — teaching. That means, in part, guiding students through canonical literature, and acclimatizing them to the norms and standards internal to academic disciplines. This is how we give them the foundation to develop scholarly expertise, themselves, should they want it. It is also how we orient them to perceive the scholarly expertise as valuable, as worthy of pursuit and preservation.

(A note on disciplines: when I was in graduate school, a fellow philosophy student observed a difference between ourselves and a friend in Comparative Literature. On encountering a new idea, our [philosophers’] reflexive response is to assess its truth, say, by considering the reasons that favour or oppose it, or pinpointing the assumptions that underly it. Our friend’s would be to locate it in a network of associations, rhyming ideas that had arisen in different contexts. These are different dispositions and different styles of reasoning — analytic vs. associative — prioritized within our respective fields. We were at that time refining, and coming more fully to inhabit, the particular cognitive skill-sets that distinguished our disciplines — ones that imprinted on us in undergraduate study.)

This is all part of the constitutive societal value of the university. A person can live a life rich in value without reading or intensely discussing Jane Austen, or John Stuart Mill, or Audre Lorde. One can engage thoughtfully with the world without a well-honed set of discipline-specific cognitive tools. But we want always for there to be some people doing these things. Our current cultural moment does not conduce to coming to them on one’s own. The university’s job is to enable it. When they’re out of fashion (which is their perennial fate), part of that job is to be their champion.

Scholarship that lacks an obvious practical application, high-level literacy, and skill sets internal to academic disciplines might not be highly marketable. (‘They must be marketable!’ say our administrators. ‘Teach them proficiency with AI tools.’) But marketability is only one kind of value. There are some things universities are uniquely suited to do. We should take seriously that it is our duty do them.

item.title: Free speech in the classroom
item.description: Remarks to the Daily Tar Heel on universities, politics, and the value we most take for granted.
item.content:encoded:
The school paper was kind enough to run a piece on my approach to teaching controversial topics—racism, affirmative action, income inequality, capitalism vs. socialism, and so forth. The piece is called “Professor Daniel Muñoz encourages discussion and disagreement,” and it’s by Jessica Baugh, who succeeded in excerpting some publishable clips from my ramblings.

Today, I thought I’d share a few of those excerpts, along with some thoughts from former students and TAs. Plus here’s a photo of me in my favorite snood.

Subscribe now

My thanks to the DTH—and to my UNC students. There is no way to have an ethos of free speech in the classroom unless students are willing to listen to each other, and I’m grateful that my students do exactly that.

Are students brainwashed?

“There’s this myth out there that contemporary college students are close[d]-minded and they only want to be reinforced in their own views, or they’re just receptacles for brainwashing,” Muñoz said. “In my experience, this is totally untrue.”

Why teachers shouldn’t bullshit (in response to hard questions)

“…nothing kills a conversation more than faking that you know the answer,” he said.

Thoughts from a student

Bahna-Neta, a sophomore from Durham with a PPE minor, said his approach helped her understand how conflicting ideas could coexist without one being right or wrong.

“It makes me more aware of the fact that people, educated people, can have strong opinions, and they might be wrong about something,” Bahna-Neta said.

Thoughts from a TA, Kendall Baker

She said Muñoz’s approach, which she said is very engaging, has influenced her own teaching.

“I try to keep in mind when I teach, like maybe I do think this paper is really boring, but if I present it like it’s the most exciting thing in the world, I’m going to get engagement from my students,” Baker said.1

On being intellectually accountable

“Even if you’re correct today, if you’re not correctable, if you’re not accountable to the facts, you’re going to be wrong pretty soon,” Muñoz said.

“The only way to be held accountable is if there’s somebody out there that wants to hold you to account,” Muñoz said. “It’s probably somebody that genuinely disagrees with you.”

On the public scrutiny of universities

In principle, it is not bad to be under scrutiny, he said, especially since professors at public universities are public employees. However, he said even as they are reformed, universities should be protected.

“I think that there’s probably no value that we take for granted more easily when we have it than freedom,” Muñoz said. “It’s like the water that you swim in or the air that you breathe, and suddenly people in the world today are finding themselves choking.”

Subscribe now

1

I got quite lucky with whom the DTH interviewed. Bahna-Neta was one of the best PPE students I’ve ever taught. Kendall was so good as a TA that Dan Wodak and I are hiring her to work for Ethics.

item.title: How to make yourself read more books
item.description: There really is one simple trick. (But you might not like it.)
item.content:encoded:
When I was a kid, I loved reading books. I read in the morning, before bed, during math class. I would even skip classes to go to the library; one teacher used to call me the Hall Wanderer.

But after high school, I found myself reading less and less. By the time I was in graduate school, I could go a whole year without reading a novel.

My sense is that this is a common thing for people of my generation. It’s also puzzling. If reading is so rewarding, why would anyone stop? Is there a way to get back into reading after taking a break, a way to fall back in love with novels, nonfiction, poetry, or whatever books grabbed you as a kid? To put it more generally, is there a way to get yourself to read more?

Thankfully, the answer is “yes.” This is one of those rare instances where a certain simple trick actually works. I can’t promise that you’ll magically end up with more free time, but you’ll win back your attention span and read more books—not just more books than you read last year, but more than you thought possible.

So what’s the trick to reading more? (Feel free to guess!)

Subscribe now

Leave a comment

Let there be no vulgar suspense. The way to read more books is to read what you enjoy—not what you’re supposed to enjoy.

Remember my story about wandering off to the library? When I was in the stacks, I wasn’t reading Plato, Aristotle, or the Encyclopedia Brittanica. I was reading Harry Potter, Garfield, and Encyclopedia Brown.

Later, in middle school, I did take a crack at Plato’s Symposium, but I gave up because I got tired of keeping track of the Greek names. Not the most flattering anecdote for a future professor, I know. But was that such a bad thing? I didn’t care back then how my reading habits would look to other people. Maybe that’s why I was able to read so much! I was reading for the sheer joy of it, following my curiosity—and if I ever lost interest, I’d put the book down.

In college, I started reading books that would fill in the gaps in my knowledge of philosophy. Some of these I savored—like Kripke’s Naming and Necessity. (I remember sneaking away during a party at Tyler Seacrest’s place to read a bit of his copy.) Other books were more about nutrition than flavor, like Moore’s supremely bland Principia Ethica.

In graduate school, I started realizing just how vast my ignorance was. Philosophy is an ancient, gigantic subject, constantly expanding in all directions. There was so much to learn! How could I justify wasting time reading novels, much less comics? I was supposed to have already read so many other things. Reading anything for fun was a disgraceful dereliction—or at least that’s how it felt. Before too long, my reading diet became the literary equivalent of Soylent and boiled cabbage. My portions shrank accordingly.

This all came to a head in my first year of grad school. I was talking to my neuroscience friend Scarlett, whom I’d met at orientation, and the conversation turned to music. I mentioned that I played guitar, which came as a surprise to her. “I thought you just did philosophy all day.” Now that came as a surprise to me! Didn’t she know that I had all these other hobbies, that I played music and read novels and such?

Then it hit me. I didn’t play music and read novels and such—or at least I hadn’t for many months.

So I resolved to start reading again. To motivate myself, I started writing the title of every book I finished on a whiteboard next to my bed. This turned out to be hugely effective, though it did bias me towards slimmer books.

Looking back, I ended up reading a ton of extremely educational books—classics in economics, literature, and philosophy (including Plato!). But almost always, the books I read weren’t quite optimal. There were usually other, more nutritious things that I was supposed to be reading instead. But I have no regrets. If I’d tried to optimize my reading habits, I’m sure I would have just lost them altogether. The perfect truly is the enemy of the good when it comes to pleasure reading, probably because chasing perfection is so dependably unpleasant.

So to anyone looking to read more: I encourage you to get in touch with your own latent curiosity and read whatever you truly want to read. Don’t inhibit your love of books. Don’t overthink it. Just let your mind wander to whatever stories or topics it wants to explore. Once you’re back in the habit of reading, you can always throw in some vitamin-rich classics.

That’s my advice, stated rather abstractly. I’ll close with some more concrete corollaries.

When I was an undergrad, I asked Sinan Dogramaci for advice about learning philosophy. He told me I should buy a bunch of books that I know are worth reading—anthologies of important papers, classics by respected scholars, and so on—and leave them around my desk. Whenever I’m bored, I can thumb through them, look for something that seems interesting, and just read that.

That’s corollary #1: if you want yourself to read something, make it easy to access. This technique applies beyond academic texts, though it does require a bit of patience. You won’t necessarily read the entire anthology tomorrow just because it’s on your shelf. Still, if you keep it close by, you’ll be that much more likely to reach for it rather than your phone.

Corollary #2 is something I discovered much too late. Your phone and laptop (etc.) are constantly crying out for your attention. If books are going to have a fighting chance, they have to be attractive. To that end, make sure you like the place where you read. Whether it’s a favorite table at a cafe or a comfy chair at home, you want an inviting, well-lit environment for reading. It’s a subtle thing that I used to never think about. But it makes a difference.

Subscribe now

In the end, there’s really no need to beat yourself up for not reading. Instead of self-flagellation, just try to make reading as easy and enjoyable as possible. It’s less painful—and more effective!
